stem: Resistance of a conductivity cell filled with \(0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution is \(100\,\Omega\). If the resistance of the same cell when filled with \(0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution is \(520\,\Omega\), calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of \(0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution. The conductivity of \(0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution is \(1.29\,\text{S/m}\).
solution:
The cell constant is given by the equation:

Cell constant \(= G^{*} =\) conductivity \(\times\) resistance

\(= 1.29\,\text{S/m} \times 100\,\Omega = 129\,\text{m}^{-1} = 1.29\,\text{cm}^{-1}\)

Conductivity of \(0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution \(=\) cell constant \(/\) resistance

\(= \dfrac{G^{*}}{R} = \dfrac{129\,\text{m}^{-1}}{520\,\Omega} = 0.248\,\text{S m}^{-1}\)

Concentration \(= 0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = 1000 \times 0.02\,\text{mol m}^{-3} = 20\,\text{mol m}^{-3}\)

Molar conductivity \(= \Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{248 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{S m}^{-1}}{20\,\text{mol m}^{-3}} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Alternatively, \(\kappa = \dfrac{1.29\,\text{cm}^{-1}}{520\,\Omega} = 0.248 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\)

and \(\Lambda_m = \kappa \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\,\text{molarity}^{-1}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.248 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}}{0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} = 124\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The printed solution spans a page break: the stem and the first half of the solution are on p-14, and the tail (from 'and \(\Lambda_m = \kappa \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\,\text{molarity}^{-1}\)' to the final \(124\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)) is at the top of p-15. Both pages are inside this band, so the solution is transcribed whole.

stem: The electrical resistance of a column of \(0.05\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{NaOH}\) solution of diameter \(1\,\text{cm}\) and length \(50\,\text{cm}\) is \(5.55 \times 10^{3}\,\text{ohm}\). Calculate its resistivity, conductivity and molar conductivity.
solution:
\(A = \pi r^{2} = 3.14 \times 0.5^{2}\,\text{cm}^{2} = 0.785\,\text{cm}^{2} = 0.785 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}\)

\(l = 50\,\text{cm} = 0.5\,\text{m}\)

\(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}\) or \(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l} = \dfrac{5.55 \times 10^{3}\,\Omega \times 0.785\,\text{cm}^{2}}{50\,\text{cm}} = 87.135\,\Omega\,\text{cm}\)

Conductivity \(= \kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \left(\dfrac{1}{87.135}\right)\,\text{S cm}^{-1} = 0.01148\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\)

Molar conductivity, \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.01148\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}}{0.05\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} = 229.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

If we want to calculate the values of different quantities in terms of 'm' instead of 'cm',

\(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l} = \dfrac{5.55 \times 10^{3}\,\Omega \times 0.785 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}}{0.5\,\text{m}} = 87.135 \times 10^{-2}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\)

\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \dfrac{100}{87.135}\,\Omega\,\text{m} = 1.148\,\text{S m}^{-1}\)

and \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{1.148\,\text{S m}^{-1}}{50\,\text{mol m}^{-3}} = 229.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
_note: Printed unit looseness carried faithfully: in the SI half of the solution the book writes the reciprocal of the resistivity as \(\kappa = \dfrac{100}{87.135}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\) — it keeps the resistivity's unit \(\Omega\,\text{m}\) where the reciprocal unit \(\text{S m}^{-1}\) belongs. The stated result \(1.148\,\text{S m}^{-1}\) is correct and carries the right unit, so only that one intermediate line's unit is wrong as printed. Every value in this solution is correct.

stem:
The molar conductivity of \(\text{KCl}\) solutions at different concentrations at \(298\,\text{K}\) are given below:

| \(c/\text{mol L}^{-1}\) | \(\Lambda_m/\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) |
|---|---|
| 0.000198 | 148.61 |
| 0.000309 | 148.29 |
| 0.000521 | 147.81 |
| 0.000989 | 147.09 |

Show that a plot between \(\Lambda_m\) and \(c^{1/2}\) is a straight line. Determine the values of \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) and \(A\) for \(\text{KCl}\).
solution:
Taking the square root of concentration we obtain:

| \(c^{1/2}/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\) | \(\Lambda_m/\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) |
|---|---|
| 0.01407 | 148.61 |
| 0.01758 | 148.29 |
| 0.02283 | 147.81 |
| 0.03145 | 147.09 |

A plot of \(\Lambda_m\) (\(y\)-axis) and \(c^{1/2}\) (\(x\)-axis) is shown in (Fig. 3.7).

It can be seen that it is nearly a straight line. From the intercept (\(c^{1/2} = 0\)), we find that

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 150.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) and

\(A = -\,\text{slope} = 87.46\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}/(\text{mol/L}^{-1})^{1/2}\).
_note: Two printed oddities, both carried faithfully rather than corrected. (1) STALE CROSS-REFERENCE: the solution says the plot 'is shown in (Fig. 3.7)', but the figure printed inside this very example box on the same page is captioned 'Fig. 2.7: Variation of \(\Lambda_m\) against \(c^{1/2}\)'. There is no Fig. 3.7 in this chapter; it is a leftover from an edition in which Electrochemistry was chapter 3 — the same stale numbering that reappears in Eg 2.7's 'Table 3.4'. (2) The unit printed for \(A\) is \((\text{mol/L}^{-1})^{1/2}\), which mixes the two conventions; it should be \((\text{mol/L})^{1/2}\), which is exactly what the book itself prints on the graph's own x-axis label on the same page and in Fig. 2.6 on p-16. No _figure attached: the stem carries its own data table and the solution states both required values, so the row is answerable without the graph.

stem: Calculate \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for \(\text{CaCl}_2\) and \(\text{MgSO}_4\) from the data given in Table 3.4.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the example cites \(\text{Table 3.4}\); the limiting molar conductivities are in \(\text{Table 2.4}\) of this chapter. Same stale renumbering as Ex 2.17 — the chapter has no Table 3.x, only 2.1 to 2.4, left over from an edition in which this was Unit 3. The worked solution below is unaffected.] We know from Kohlrausch law that

\(\Lambda_{m(\text{CaCl}_2)}^{\circ} = \lambda_{\text{Ca}^{2+}}^{\circ} + 2\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{\circ} = 119.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} + 2(76.3)\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(= (119.0 + 152.6)\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 271.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(\Lambda_{m(\text{MgSO}_4)}^{\circ} = \lambda_{\text{Mg}^{2+}}^{\circ} + \lambda_{\text{SO}_4^{2-}}^{\circ} = 106.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} + 160.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(= 266\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
_note: STALE CROSS-REFERENCE carried faithfully: the stem cites 'Table 3.4', but every table in this chapter is numbered 2.x. The table meant is Table 2.4, 'Limiting Molar Conductivity for some Ions in Water at 298 K', printed on p-18 — verified: it carries exactly the four values this solution uses (\(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) 119.0, \(\text{Cl}^{-}\) 76.3, \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) 106.0, \(\text{SO}_4^{2-}\) 160.0). The book contradicts itself one page apart: the prose on p-18 introducing that table correctly says 'are given in Table 2.4', while this stem on p-19 calls it 3.4. Same leftover chapter-3 numbering as Eg 2.6's '(Fig. 3.7)'. No _figure attached: the book's own solution quotes every ionic conductivity it needs, so the row ships answerable without the table.

stem: \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for \(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{HCl}\) and \(\text{NaAc}\) are \(126.4\), \(425.9\) and \(91.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) respectively. Calculate \(\Lambda^{\circ}\) for \(\text{HAc}\).
_note: Minor printed inconsistency, carried faithfully: the last sentence of the stem asks for \(\Lambda^{\circ}\) (no \(m\) subscript) where the rest of the stem and the whole solution use \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\). Nothing turns on it — the quantity asked for is unambiguous.

stem: The conductivity of \(0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) acetic acid is \(4.95 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\). Calculate its dissociation constant if \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for acetic acid is \(390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
solution:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{4.95 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}}{0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} \times \dfrac{1000\,\text{cm}^{3}}{\text{L}} = 48.15\,\text{S cm}^{3}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{48.15\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}}{390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}} = 0.1233\)

\(k = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{(1-\alpha)} = \dfrac{0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times (0.1233)^{2}}{1 - 0.1233} = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
_note: PRINTED UNIT ERROR carried faithfully (checked at 5x zoom on the page, not read off the text layer): the first line of the book's solution ends '\(= 48.15\,\text{S cm}^{3}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)' — a CUBIC centimetre, where molar conductivity requires \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). The book refutes itself on the very next line, where the same 48.15 is written \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) inside the \(\alpha\) ratio, and the dimensional analysis of \(\kappa/c \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\) gives \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Only the exponent is wrong; the value 48.15 and every downstream result are correct. Left exactly as printed for the answer-key cross-check to adjudicate rather than silently corrected. Secondary: the book writes the dissociation constant as a lower-case \(k\) in the final step, where its own equation (2.27) on this same page calls it \(K_a\).
